evidence: Britannica: a film is 'a series of still photographs on film projected onto a screen using light in rapid succession', creating the illusion of continuous movement.

IEEE Spectrum: the conclusive experiment took place on 19 June 1878 at Stanford's Palo Alto farm, with thread-triggered cameras lined up along the track; the images were then shown on a zoopraxiscope.

Institut Lumiere: after demonstrations from 22 March 1895, the Cinematographe had its commercial run from 28 December 1895 at the Grand Cafe, boulevard des Capucines; Britannica's Lumiere article gives the same Grand Cafe showing.

Britannica: television 'delivers moving images and sound electronically from a source to a receiver'; General Electric began regular experimental broadcasts in 1928 with an Alexanderson-designed system.
Britannica: film requires 'contributions from nearly all the other arts as well as countless technical skills (for example, in sound recording, photography, and optics).'
Britannica: film developed as 'a means of artistic expression in such areas as acting, directing, screenwriting, cinematography, costume and set design, and music.'

Britannica (film editing): 'the process of trimming and piecing together lengths of film in order to make an artistically concise and complete motion picture'; judging each shot's length is part of that trimming.
Britannica: phi was first described in 1912 in Wertheimer's paper; he reportedly noticed it in 1910 on a train near Frankfurt watching alternating railway signal lights.
Britannica: in beta movement 'a series of still images show[s] an object in a slightly different position in each image' and the object is seen to move.
Britannica: phi and beta movement explain 'how such technologies as animation, film, and electronic displays create the illusion of continuous motion from a sequence of still images.'
Anderson and Anderson: the visual system 'seemingly cannot distinguish between short-range apparent motion and real motion. To the visual system the motion in a motion picture is real motion.'

Anderson and Anderson: fusion of images 'could produce only the superimposition of successive views'; they note 'the obvious inadequacy of the explanation, coupled with its recurrence in film literature for almost a century.'

Anderson and Anderson separate 'the fusing of the flickering light, called flicker fusion in the literature of perceptual psychology, and the appearance of motion which is referred to as apparent motion.'
Britannica: 'the human brain will perceive an illusion of continuous movement from a succession of still images exposed at a rate above 15 frames per second.'
Britannica (sound era section): 'silent cameras had been mainly hand-cranked at rates averaging 16 to 18 frames per second.'
Britannica: 'there was wide variation in the speed at which silent films were photographed and projected.'
Britannica: 'sound necessitated standardization of the frame rate. In 1927 the speed was standardized at 24 frames per second, or 90 feet per minute for 35-mm film.'
Britannica: cameras 'were motorized in 1929 to run at an even speed of 24 frames per second.'
Malkiewicz and Mullen sample: action shot at 12 fps and projected at 24 takes half the time; 'movements filmed at 36 fps or faster acquire a slow, dreamy quality at 24 fps on the screen.'

IEEE Spectrum: Stanford 'challenged Muybridge to settle the old dispute about whether all four of a horse's legs are off the ground at one time during a gallop.' (Britannica phrases Stanford's original question as a trotting horse.)

Smarthistory essay (reprinted): photographs at Stanford's Palo Alto track on June 19, 1878; Sallie Gardner ran past 'Muybridge's battery of twelve cameras' and tripped threads to release the shutters. LoC's catalog title also dates the series 19 June 1878, Palo Alto track.
Britannica: 'the shutters of the cameras were released by the breaking of their attached threads.'

IEEE Spectrum: Sallie Gardner 'clearly had all four hooves off the ground', but not as in paintings such as Gericault's Derby at Epsom with legs extended; it occurred 'when the horse's legs were beneath its body.'
Britannica: the zoopraxiscope was 'a lantern he developed that projected images in rapid succession onto a screen'; 'an important predecessor of the modern cinema.'

LoC (read via the page's JSON view): Zoopraxiscope images came from multiple cameras; 'a camera in the Edison laboratories capable of recording successive images in a single camera was a more practical, cost-effective breakthrough that influenced all subsequent motion picture devices.'
LoC: Muybridge visited the West Orange laboratory in February 1888 and proposed combining the Zoopraxiscope with the phonograph; 'Edison decided not to participate in such a partnership.'
LoC: Edison filed a caveat on October 17, 1888, for a device to 'do for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear'; he called it a 'Kinetoscope.'

LoC: Dickson was given the task in June 1889 and 'apparently performed the bulk of the experimentation, leading most modern scholars to assign Dickson with the major credit'; Edison 'took sole credit.'

LoC quoting Robinson: 'an upright wooden cabinet, 18 in. x 27 in. x 4 ft. high, with a peephole'; film in a band of about 50 feet drawn at a continuous rate over a lamp, with a revolving shutter giving a flash so brief the frame appeared frozen.

LoC: 'The first Kinetoscope parlor, owned by the Holland Brothers, opened on April 14, 1894, in New York. Five machines were placed in a row, and a customer could view the films in each for a total of 25 cents.'

LoC: 'Edison was slow to develop a projection system at this time, since the single-user Kinetoscopes were very profitable. However, films projected for large audiences could generate more profits because fewer machines were needed.'
LoC: 'Sales of Kinetoscopes slowed as projected motion pictures began to overtake the peep show machines in 1895.'

LoC: the Vitascope was 'invented by Thomas Armat and C. Francis Jenkins' and advertised as an Edison invention; its 'first theatrical exhibition was on April 23, 1896, at Koster and Bial's Music Hall in New York City.'

Britannica: 'a showing at the Grand Cafe on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris brought wide public acclaim and the beginning of cinema history'; Institut Lumiere dates the commercial run from 28 December 1895.

Institut Lumiere: a small Paris audience attended the first demonstration on 22 March 1895 at the Societe d'encouragement pour l'Industrie nationale, followed by other demonstrations before the 28 December showings.
LoC: Woodville Latham and his sons 'created the Eidoloscope projector which was presented publicly in April 1895'; LoC does not name the city, but Latham's showings were in New York.

Britannica: Antoine 'was invited to a showing of Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope in Paris', which set Louis and Auguste to work on combining animation with projection. Institut Lumiere: this was possible from September 1894, and their aim was showing moving images to a public, not individually.
Institut Lumiere: the device, 'pesant moins de 5 kg', combined 'les fonctions de camera, tireuse et projecteur', which 'a grandement facilite les voyages des operateurs.'
Britannica: their first films 'recorded everyday French life', e.g. the arrival of a train; it also names La Sortie des ouvriers de l'usine Lumiere (1895).
Britannica: 'Beginning in 1896 they sent a trained crew of innovative cameraman-projectionists to cities throughout the world to show films and shoot new material.'

Britannica: 'a loose adaptation of Jules Verne's novel From the Earth to the Moon', 'about 825 feet... or 14 minutes', in which the spacecraft 'strikes the man in the moon in the eye.'
Britannica: Melies employed 'various camera tricks, such as stop motion and superimposition.'
Britannica: it 'was one of the first films to achieve international distribution and was instrumental in establishing narrative films as a mainstream cinematic product.'
Britannica: directed by Edwin S. Porter for the Edison Manufacturing Company, running about 12 minutes; LoC's catalog gives 11:54 at 18 fps.
Britannica: combines 14 separate shots; bandits force a telegraph operator to stop the train, rob it and its passengers, and are tracked down by a posse.

National Archives blog: Porter 'used cross-cutting to show that two events were occurring simultaneously... when Porter shifts back and forth between the tied up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train.'
Britannica: 'the first narrative film to successfully establish continuity of action', a 'dramatic departure from the frontally composed, theatrical staging' of its contemporaries.
LoC catalog (JSON view): 'Filmed during November 1903 at Edison's New York studio, in Essex County Park in New Jersey... and along the Lackawanna Railroad.'
LoC: 'a famous close-up shot of Justus D. Barnes in the role of the outlaw, shooting straight at the camera, a scene that could be shown at the beginning or end of the film.'
Britannica: its popularity 'tapped into the public's fascination with the Old West', establishing westerns as a Hollywood mainstay.
Britannica: intermittent movement is 'the motion of film where it advances one or more frames at a time, with stationary periods in between.'
Britannica: in the camera, 'a claw-type mechanism, sometimes a dual-fork claw that pulls down four sprocket holes at a time.'
Britannica: the four-slot Maltese cross, introduced in the 1890s, 'provides the intermittent Geneva movement that stops each frame of the continuously moving film in front of the picture aperture.'

Institut Lumiere: a process 'tres similaire a celui de la machine a coudre'; an eccentric cam drives claws in the perforations, and '2 tours par seconde correspond a l'avance intermittente du film de 16 images par seconde.'

Malkiewicz and Mullen: the rotating shutter 'closes over the aperture, stopping exposure and allowing the movement to advance the film to the next frame'; Britannica's intermittent entry says the same.
Malkiewicz and Mullen: 'Flicker happens when the series of still images are not being flashed quickly enough for the viewer to perceive the light and image as being continuously on.'
Malkiewicz and Mullen: projectors generally 'use a twin-bladed shutter'; 'even if the movie was shot and then projected at 24 fps, the viewer is seeing forty-eight flashes per second.'
LoC: companies 'frequently copied, or duped, each other's films'; the Edison Company 'began to copyright films regularly in October 1896', sent as 'positive image paper photographic rolls.'
LoC: 'These paper prints, along with those received from other companies, accumulated to form the collection known today as the Library of Congress's Paper Print Collection.'

LoC: 'The earliest copyrighted film that still survives is Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze, January 7, 1894'; it was submitted not on celluloid 'but rather as a series of positive photographic prints.'
